title: 2 Kings 8:16–29
context: The narrative turns to Judah. Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat reigns eight years, marries a daughter of Ahab’s house, and does evil, yet the LORD does not destroy Judah for David’s sake, because he promised David a lamp always (8:19; compare 1 Kings 11:36; 15:4). Edom and Libnah revolt. His son Ahaziah, whose mother Athaliah is of Omri’s line, reigns one year, also walks in the way of Ahab’s house, and joins Joram of Israel against Hazael at Ramoth Gilead; the closing scene in Jezreel sets up Jehu’s revolt in chapter 9. Several regnal and parallel details are stated here plainly without harmonization. 8:16 dates Jehoram of Judah to the fifth year of Joram of Israel and still names Jehoshaphat as king, while 1:17 and 3:1 date Joram of Israel’s accession differently; the text does not explain how these figures relate, and some readers propose overlapping reigns. 8:25 dates Ahaziah’s accession to Joram’s twelfth year, while 9:29 says the eleventh. 8:26 gives Ahaziah’s age as twenty-two, while 2 Chronicles 22:2 gives forty-two. Chronicles also adds some details, such as Jehoram’s killing of his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:4). Both traditions treat the reign evaluations and the promise to David as shared ground.

verses.text: In the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat being king of Judah then, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah began to reign.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat begins to reign over Judah in the fifth year of Joram of Israel. Arminian readers note the shift to Judah’s royal record. The regnal details here are difficult to align with other notices, as the context explains, and they do not press the chronology for theological conclusions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly acknowledge the chronological questions without forcing a harmony, and they focus on the narrative’s purpose of tracing Judah’s kings under God’s covenant with David. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a regnal notice and handle its chronological difficulty honestly.

verses.text: He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign. He reigned eight years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoram is thirty-two when he begins to reign and reigns eight years in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the brief notice, which matches 2 Chronicles 21:5. The narrative is concerned less with the length of his reign than with the way he walks before the LORD, as the next verse shows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly treat the verse as a straightforward regnal notice. The agreement with 2 Chronicles 21:5 and 21:20 is noted plainly. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical detail and see the real emphasis falling on Jehoram’s evaluation in the following verses.

verses.text: He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did Ahab’s house, for he married Ahab’s daughter. He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoram walks in the way of the kings of Israel, like Ahab’s house, because he married Ahab’s daughter. Arminian readers note how a marriage alliance shapes a king’s choices and leads him into evil. He remains responsible for his own walk before the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the corrupting influence of Ahab’s house and Jehoram’s responsibility for his sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the evaluation as a clear verdict that Jehoram did evil in the LORD’s sight, and both see in it a warning about alliances that draw God’s people away from him.

verses.text: However, the LORD would not destroy Judah, for David his servant’s sake, as he promised him to give to him a lamp for his children always.
verses.arminianNotes: Yet the LORD will not destroy Judah, for David’s sake, because he promised David a lamp always. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to his covenant promise even when a king is unfaithful. God’s patience preserves Judah, though it does not excuse Jehoram’s sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same faithfulness and stress that the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:16) rests on God’s commitment, not on the king’s merit. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a striking statement of covenant faithfulness, in which God keeps his word to David despite his descendants’ failures.

verses.text: In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah, and made a king over themselves.
verses.arminianNotes: Edom revolts from Judah and makes its own king. Arminian readers note that the loss of control over Edom follows directly on the evaluation of Jehoram’s evil reign. The narrator records the political setback without spelling out its cause here, though 2 Chronicles 21:10 links a revolt to his forsaking the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the revolt within God’s governance of history and note the connection the Chronicler draws (2 Chronicles 21:10). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a historical notice of decline and are cautious about assigning more cause than each text states.

verses.text: Then Joram crossed over to Zair, and all his chariots with him; and he rose up by night and struck the Edomites who surrounded him with the captains of the chariots; and the people fled to their tents.
verses.arminianNotes: Joram crosses to Zair with his chariots and strikes the Edomites by night, but his own people flee to their tents. Arminian readers note the mixed outcome: a tactical escape that does not restore Judah’s rule. Human effort here does not reverse the decline.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a limited success that cannot undo Edom’s revolt. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical narrative of a difficult campaign and see no theological dispute in it; 2 Chronicles 21:9 records the same night battle without naming Zair or mentioning the people fleeing.

verses.text: So Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time.
verses.arminianNotes: Edom remains in revolt “to this day,” and Libnah revolts at the same time. Arminian readers note the lasting consequences of Jehoram’s reign. Losses at the edges of the kingdom show that unfaithfulness has real effects, even while God preserves Judah for David’s sake.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same losses as part of God’s discipline of an unfaithful king, held within his commitment to David’s line. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s covenant faithfulness and his discipline of sin operate together in Judah’s history.

verses.text: The rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Joram’s acts are recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Arminian readers note the narrator’s reference to a fuller royal record, which shows that the book is selective. Its focus is on how a king walked before the LORD rather than on every detail of his reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the selective, theological purpose of the narrative, which points readers elsewhere for more detail. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a standard closing formula and agree that it raises no point of doctrinal difference between them.

verses.text: Joram slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in David’s city; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Joram dies, is buried in David’s city, and Ahaziah his son reigns in his place. Arminian readers note the continuity of David’s line despite Joram’s evil. God’s promise of a lamp (8:19) is visibly kept as the throne passes to the next generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same continuity as evidence of God’s faithfulness to David. 2 Chronicles 21:20 adds that he died with no one’s regret and was not buried in the tombs of the kings. Shared ground: both traditions read the succession as the covenant promise preserved through an unworthy king.

verses.text: In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah began to reign.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaziah son of Jehoram begins to reign in the twelfth year of Joram of Israel. Arminian readers note the regnal notice and the difference from 2 Kings 9:29, which gives the eleventh year, recorded plainly in the context. They do not build conclusions on the chronology.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly acknowledge the difference without forcing a harmony, and they read the verse as part of the narrative’s careful tracking of the two kingdoms. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as a regnal notice and handle its chronological detail honestly.

verses.text: Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign; and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Athaliah the daughter of Omri king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaziah is twenty-two when he begins to reign and reigns one year; his mother is Athaliah, of Omri’s line. Arminian readers note the significance of his mother’s family for what follows. The difference from 2 Chronicles 22:2, which gives forty-two, is recorded plainly in the context.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Athaliah’s lineage, which anticipates her later seizure of power (2 Kings 11:1). They acknowledge the age difference with Chronicles without forced harmony. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a regnal notice that introduces Ahab’s house into Judah’s royal line.

verses.text: He walked in the way of Ahab’s house and did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, as did Ahab’s house, for he was the son-in-law of Ahab’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaziah walks in the way of Ahab’s house and does evil, for he is related to Ahab’s house by marriage. Arminian readers note how family ties shape his choices, while he remains responsible for following that way. 2 Chronicles 22:3–4 adds that his mother and Ahab’s house counseled him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the corrupting influence of Ahab’s house and Ahaziah’s responsibility for his evil. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a clear evaluation of an evil king and see in it a warning about the influence of ungodly counsel and alliances.

verses.text: He went with Joram the son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth Gilead, and the Syrians wounded Joram.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaziah goes with Joram of Israel to fight Hazael at Ramoth Gilead, and Joram is wounded. Arminian readers note that Hazael, whose rise was foretold in 8:12–13, now appears as Israel’s enemy. Ahaziah’s alliance with Ahab’s house draws him into danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrative connecting Hazael’s rise to the trouble now facing Israel and Judah. 2 Chronicles 22:5 adds that Ahaziah followed the counsel of Ahab’s house in going. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking the prophecy about Hazael to the events of the kings’ reigns.

verses.text: King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel from the wounds which the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. Ahaziah the son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.
verses.arminianNotes: Joram returns to Jezreel to recover, and Ahaziah goes down to visit him. Arminian readers note that the scene sets up the events of chapter 9, where both kings will meet Jehu. Ahaziah’s choice to stay close to Ahab’s house places him where judgment will fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Chronicles 22:7 says Ahaziah’s destruction was of God, through his going to Joram. They see God’s purpose working through Ahaziah’s own choices. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparing for Jehu’s judgment on Ahab’s house, with Ahaziah responsible for his alliance.
